{{Short description|Probabilistic model}}
'''Impartial culture''' ('''IC'''), or the '''culture of indifference''',<ref name=":1">{{cite journal |last1=Van Deemen |first1=Adrian |title=On the empirical relevance of Condorcet's paradox |journal=Public Choice |date=March 2014 |volume=158 |issue=3–4 |pages=311–330 |doi=10.1007/s11127-013-0133-3 |s2cid=154862595|quote=The impartial culture assumption has been criticized extensively as being implausible and empirically irrelevant}}</ref> is a [[probabilistic model]] used in [[social choice theory]] for analyzing [[Ranked voting|ranked]] [[Electoral system|voting method]] rules.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal |last1=Eğecioğlu |first1=Ömer |last2=Giritligil |first2=Ayça E. |title=The Impartial, Anonymous, and Neutral Culture Model: A Probability Model for Sampling Public Preference Structures |journal=The Journal of Mathematical Sociology |date=October 2013 |volume=37 |issue=4 |pages=203–222 |doi=10.1080/0022250X.2011.597012 |s2cid=17266150 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Guilbaud |first1=Georges-Théodule |title=Les théories de l'intérêt général et le problème logique de l'agrégation |trans-title=Theories of general interest and the logical problem of aggregation |language=fr |journal=Revue économique |date=2012 |volume=63 |issue=4 |page=659 |doi=10.3917/reco.634.0659 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

The model is understood to be unrealistic, and not a good representation of real-world voting behavior, however, it is useful for mathematical comparisons of voting methods under reproducible, worst-case scenarios.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lehtinen |first1=Aki |last2=Kuorikoski |first2=Jaakko |title=Unrealistic Assumptions in Rational Choice Theory |journal=Philosophy of the Social Sciences |date=June 2007 |volume=37 |issue=2 |pages=115–138 |doi=10.1177/0048393107299684 |s2cid=145169622 |quote=…Using unrealistic assumptions may thus have a reasonable methodological function even if we know how to describe reality in a more realistic way…}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tsetlin |first1=Ilia |last2=Regenwetter |first2=Michel |last3=Grofman |first3=Bernard |title=The impartial culture maximizes the probability of majority cycles |journal=Social Choice and Welfare |date=1 December 2003 |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=387–398 |doi=10.1007/s00355-003-0269-z |s2cid=15488300|quote=it is widely acknowledged that the impartial culture is unrealistic … the impartial culture is the worst case scenario}}</ref><ref>{{cite CiteSeerX |last1=Tideman |first1=T. Nicolaus |last2=Plassmann |first2=Florenz |title=The Source of Election Results: An Empirical Analysis of Statistical Models of Voter Behavior |date=2008 |citeseerx=10.1.1.504.3181|quote=Voting theorists generally acknowledge that they consider this model to be unrealistic}}</ref><ref name=":1" /><ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-03107-6_1 |chapter=Voting Paradoxes and Their Probabilities |title=Voting Paradoxes and Group Coherence |series=Studies in Choice and Welfare |year=2011 |last1=Gehrlein |first1=William V. |last2=Lepelley |first2=Dominique |pages=1–47 |isbn=978-3-642-03106-9|quote=if we use conditions that tend to exaggerate the likelihood of observing paradoxes and find that the probability is small with such calculations, the paradox is assuredly very unlikely to be observed in reality.}}</ref>

The model assumes that each voter provides a complete strict ranking of all the candidates (with no equal rankings or blanks), which is drawn from a set of all possible rankings.  For <math>m</math> candidates, there are <math>m!</math> possible strict rankings ([[permutation]]s).<ref name=":0" />

There are three variations of the model that use different subsets of the full set of possible rankings, so that different election permutations are drawn with different probabilities:

== Impartial culture ==
This model assumes that each voter's ranking is randomly selected from a uniform distribution.  If these are chosen by <math>n</math> voters, there are thus <math>m!^n</math> possible elections ("preference profiles").<ref name=":0" />

== Impartial anonymous culture ==
This reduces the set of possible elections by eliminating those that are equivalent if the voter identities are unknown.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{cite web |last1=Veselova |first1=Yuliya A. |title=Comparing Probabilistic Models: IC, IAC, IANC |website=Editorial Express |date=2014 |url=https://editorialexpress.com/cgi-bin/conference/download.cgi?db_name=SSCWatBC&paper_id=359 |s2cid=33200881}}</ref>  For example, the two-candidate, three-voter election {A>B, A>B, B>A} is equivalent to the election where the second and third voters swap votes: {A>B, B>A, A>B}, and so all variations on this set of votes are only included once.  The set of all such elections is called the anonymous equivalence class (AEC), and if the strict rankings are being chosen by <math>n</math> voters, there are  <math>\left ( \frac {n+m!-1} {m!-1} \right )</math> possible elections.<ref name=":0" />

This is also referred to as the "Dirichlet" or "simplex" model.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Quas |first1=Anthony |title=Anomalous outcomes in preferential voting |journal=Stochastics and Dynamics |date=March 2004 |volume=04 |issue=1 |pages=95–105 |doi=10.1142/S0219493704000912|quote=In the ''simplex model'', an assumption is made that vote allocations are uniformly distributed on the simplex.}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Tideman |first1=T. Nicolaus |last2=Plassmann |first2=Florenz |title=The Structure of the Election-Generating Universe |website=London School of Economics and Political Science |page=5 |date=2010 |url=https://www.lse.ac.uk/cpnss/assets/documents/voting-power-and-procedures/workshops/2010/duBaffy2010-Plassmann.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=de Mouzon |first1=Olivier |last2=Laurent |first2=Thibault |last3=Le Breton |first3=Michel |last4=Lepelley |first4=Dominique |title=The theoretical Shapley–Shubik probability of an election inversion in a toy symmetric version of the US presidential electoral system |journal=Social Choice and Welfare |date=March 2020 |volume=54 |issue=2–3 |pages=363–395 |doi=10.1007/s00355-018-1162-0 |s2cid=148626981 |url=https://publications.ut-capitole.fr/26416/1/wp_tse_671.pdf|quote=It can be shown that IAC is equivalent to the assumption that the preferences of the voters are independent and identically distributed according to a multinomial distribution conditional on a prior uniform draw … This prior is a special case of a Dirichlet distribution.}}</ref>

== Impartial, anonymous, and neutral culture ==
This reduces the set of possible elections further, by eliminating those that are equivalent if the candidate identities are unknown.  For example, the two-candidate, three-voter election {A>B, A>B, B>A} is equivalent to the election where the two candidates are swapped: {B>A, B>A, A>B}.<ref name=":0" />
